hero.title: Am I in a controlling relationship?
hero.description: Twenty questions about your freedom in the relationship: your friends, your money, your choices, your voice. To put words on what you may no longer dare to say. Instant and confidential result.
hero.subtitle: Free, confidential, instant result

section1.title: Coercive control isn't one argument too many
section1.intro: We picture control with shouting and bans. Most of the time, it doesn't look like that.
section1.p1: Coercive control is a relationship in which one of the two gradually takes power over the other's life. Not all at once. Through remarks, sulking, "I'm only saying this for your own good", outbursts you learn to avoid. After a few months or a few years, the person being controlled no longer decides much on their own. And often, they don't realise it.
section1.p2: That's precisely what makes it hard to see from the inside. Each thing taken separately has an explanation: he's jealous because he's been hurt, she controls the money because she's better at it, he doesn't want to see my friends because they don't like him. Put together, those explanations draw something else.
section1.p3: This test doesn't look at your partner. It looks at you: what you still dare to do, say, think. It doesn't replace a professional and it doesn't make a diagnosis. It's there to answer a simple question. Am I still free in my relationship?
section1.quote: "The first sign of control is that you start wondering whether you're allowed."

section2.title: Freedom or control: the table
section2.intro: The same subject, seen in a free relationship and in a controlling one.
section2.row1Level: You see them when you want
section2.row1Analysis: You see them less, and it's always "because of them"
section2.row2Level: It's yours to use, big choices are made together
section2.row2Analysis: You justify ordinary purchases, or you have to ask
section2.row3Analysis: It's checked, and you delete messages just in case
section2.row4Level: You can have two versions and laugh about it
section2.row4Analysis: You're told you're making it up, and you end up doubting
section2.row5Analysis: You walk on eggshells, and you're afraid

section3.title: The mechanisms you recognise afterwards
section3.p1: People who have come out of a controlling relationship almost all describe the same stages. At the time, none of them is clearly visible.
section3.sub1P1: It starts with a remark about a friend, then about your family, then about your colleagues. Nobody is good enough, everyone means you harm or influences you. Little by little, you see fewer people, to avoid the arguments. And one day, only he or she is left to tell you what's true.
section3.sub2P1: "I never said that", "you're making it up", "you always exaggerate". When these sentences come back often, you start to stop trusting yourself. You write things down, you replay conversations in your head, you apologise for facts you're actually sure of. It has a name, gaslighting, and it's one of the most powerful levers of control.
section3.sub3P1: They hurt you and, at the end of the discussion, you're the one apologising. You "provoked" them, you "misunderstood", you're "too sensitive". Once, it happens to everyone. When it's always in the same direction, it's no longer an argument, it's a mechanism.
section3.sub4P1: Not necessarily fear of being hit. Fear of the reaction, of the sulk that will last three days, of the cold anger, of "you'll pay for this". You adjust your clothes, your schedule, your words. You walk on eggshells. That's where control shows best: in everything you do to stop it blowing up.

section4.title: Control, toxic relationship, narcissistic partner: three different questions
section4.p1: These three terms often come up together, and they don't mean the same thing. This test looks at what the relationship does to you. Another one looks at how the two of you function together: arguments, respect, jealousy, communication. A third looks at your partner's profile, and the very particular mechanics they set up.
section4.p2: You can be controlled without the other person being a narcissist: pathological jealousy, very strong anxiety, an upbringing where "the man decides" or "the woman runs the house" are sometimes enough. And you can live a toxic relationship, with arguments and hurtful words on both sides, without control. Control is when the relationship is no longer between equals, and only one of the two is afraid.
section4.tip: If you're hesitating between the three, start with this one. It's the only one that asks nothing about the other person, only about you, and it's often the easiest to do honestly.

section5.title: Why people don't leave
section5.intro: "But why do you stay?" is the most asked question, and the most unfair. Here are the real reasons, and none of them is weakness.
section5.pillar1Title: Because it wasn't always like this
section5.pillar1Text: The beginning was often wonderful, too wonderful even. You wait for that person to come back, and from time to time they do, for a few days. Those good moments help you hold on. They're part of the mechanism.
section5.pillar2Title: Because you no longer trust yourself
section5.pillar2Text: After months of being told you exaggerate, you end up believing it. Leaving takes self-trust, and that's exactly what control damaged first. It often mixes with an emotional dependency that was already there, and that it fed.
section5.pillar3Text: Of their reaction, of what they would do, to you, to the children, or to themselves. That fear is often well founded, and it has to be prepared for: you don't leave a controlling relationship on a whim, you leave it with a plan and people around you.
section5.pillar4Text: Isolation has done its work. Friends have drifted away, family has been kept at a distance, and the idea of starting over alone is scarier than staying. That's the first thread to weave back, well before deciding anything.

section6.title: Where to start, depending on your result
section6.p1: There's no urgency to decide everything tonight. There is an urgency to stop being alone with this.
section6.sub1P1: A friend, a brother, a colleague. Someone you can tell the facts to, not your analysis, just the facts. The eyes of someone who knew you before put things back in their place faster than any test.
section6.sub2P1: One sentence, one date. Not to build a case, but to stop doubting your memory. When you reread three months of notes, what seemed "not that bad" day to day takes on its real weight.
section6.sub3P1: A psychologist, a charity, a doctor. Domestic abuse helplines answer psychological abuse too, not only physical violence: in the UK, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline on 0808 2000 247 (free, 24 hours) and the Men's Advice Line on 0808 801 0327; in the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline on 1-800-799-7233. They're free and confidential.
section6.sub4Title: Don't announce anything before you're ready
section6.sub4P1: If your result is high and you're afraid, don't tell your partner you took this test, or that you're thinking of leaving. Support organisations repeat it: the riskiest moment is when the other person understands they're losing control. You prepare first, you announce afterwards, and never alone.
section6.tip: If you're in danger, call 999 in the UK or 911 in the US. A controlling relationship can tip over, and nobody will blame you for calling for nothing.

section7.title: How this test works
section7.p1: Twenty questions about your everyday life, four answers each time, from the freest to the most constrained. You answer for yourself, about the last six months. There's nothing to guess about your partner, and your answers aren't stored.
section7.p2: Some questions weigh more: the ones about fear, isolation, money and doubting your own memory, because they're the pillars of control. And an answer that describes fear, surveillance or physical violence raises the result by a level on its own, whatever the rest says: sulking now and then and raising a hand can't weigh the same. The score places you on four levels, from "free in your relationship" to "control is established", each time with what it means and a first thing to do.
section7.tip: This test isn't a diagnosis, and it doesn't replace someone trained for these situations. If your result frightens you, that's already information. Take it seriously, and talk to someone about it.

seo.faqTitle: The questions people ask about coercive control
seo.faq1Q: What is coercive control in a relationship?
seo.faq1A: It's a relationship where one of the two takes power over the other's life, gently and over time: their friends, their money, their choices, all the way to how they think. There isn't necessarily shouting or hitting. There's fear, doubt and an isolation that grows. The person being controlled often only realises afterwards.
seo.faq2Q: What are the signs that you're being controlled?
seo.faq2A: You see your loved ones less, you justify your spending or your outings, you adjust your words and your clothes to avoid a reaction, you often apologise without knowing why anymore, and you doubt your memory. The surest sign: you're afraid of their reaction, and you organise your life around that fear.
seo.faq3Q: Can you be controlled without physical violence?
seo.faq3A: Yes, and it's even the most common case. Coercive control is psychological abuse. In several countries, including England and Wales and France, it's a criminal offence in its own right, even without a single blow. Domestic abuse helplines answer these situations too.
seo.faq4Q: Can I be controlled without my partner being a narcissist?
seo.faq4A: Yes. The narcissistic partner is a precise profile, and quite a rare one. Control, on the other hand, can come from pathological jealousy, from very strong anxiety, from an upbringing where one of the two "gives the orders", or from a mix of all that. For you, what matters isn't labelling the other person. It's measuring what the relationship does to you.
seo.faq5Q: How do you get out of a controlling relationship?
seo.faq5A: Rarely alone, and rarely all at once. You start by finding a connection outside, a trusted person, then a professional. You write down what happens so you stop doubting yourself. And you prepare the departure before announcing it, because the moment the other person feels they're losing control is the most delicate. Specialist organisations support exactly that.
seo.faq6A: It's a self-observation tool, not a diagnosis. It helps you put words on things and see a whole where, day to day, you only see isolated details. A high result proves nothing legally and doesn't replace a professional's opinion. But if you recognised yourself in most of the questions, that's not nothing, and it deserves talking about.
